🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.

🎙 Newly identified remains of Minab school massacre victims laid to rest

📌 Bandar Abbas, IRNA – The southern Iranian city of Minab has held a funeral ceremony for 34 victims of the Shajareh Tayyebeh School massacre, whose remains were identified after months of recovery efforts and DNA testing.

The victims’ remains were carried through the city in a ceremony attended by bereaved families, local officials, and other groups of people from across Hormuzgan Province on Wednesday.
​
The funeral procession began at Imam Khomeini Square and ended at Minab’s Martyrs’ Cemetery, where the remains were laid to rest.
​
According to Ataollah Navaki, director general of the Foundation of Martyrs and Veterans Affairs in Hormozgan Province, 68 pieces of remains belonging to the 34 victims were recovered from the rubble of the school over more than four months of search operations.
​
The recovered remains were sent to specialized genetic laboratories for identification, he said. After the victims were conclusively identified and with the consent of their families, the remains were prepared to be reunited with the bodies that had previously been buried, he added.
​
A tragedy etched in memory
​
Hormozgan Deputy Governor for Political, Security and Social Affairs Ahmad Nafisi said the ceremony was more than a funeral, describing it as a reaffirmation of the collective memory of a people who would never forget the “deliberate killing” of innocent children at the school.
​
“The people of Minab have turned out in large numbers, delivering a resounding response to the enemies who thought the passage of time would make this tragedy fade from memory,” he said, adding that the victims’ deaths had further strengthened the roots of the Islamic Revolution in the region.
​
The massacre at Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab took place on February 1, 2026, the first day of the recent US-Israeli war on Iran. Airstrikes hit the school in the early hours of the war, killing 168 students, teachers and school staff.

🎙 Iran-Pakistan rail link to become strategic regional game changer: Official

📌 Islamabad, IRNA – Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni has described the planned railway connection between Iran and Pakistan as a strategic project that could transform regional transportation, strengthen bilateral trade, and improve access to destinations across the region and beyond.

Speaking on Wednesday during a meeting in Islamabad with Pakistan’s Minister for Railways Muhammad Hanif Abbasi, the Iranian minister highlighted the growing cooperation between the two neighboring countries and emphasized the importance of expanding rail connectivity.
​
The meeting was attended by Pakistan’s Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, the governor of Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan Province, senior Iranian Foreign Ministry officials, and Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan as well.
​
Momeni said Iran and Pakistan share deep historical and cultural ties, adding that bilateral relations have expanded significantly over the past two years. He also thanked the Pakistani government and people for their support during the recent imposed war against Iran and praised Islamabad’s efforts to promote regional peace.
​
“The two countries have the potential to expand their cooperation far beyond its current level. Closer synergy could help advance their shared interests, particularly by promoting development and prosperity for people living along their common border,” the Iranian minister said.
​
He noted that the launch of the ECO container train and the completion of cross-border rail infrastructure would substantially enhance trade and regional connectivity.
​
The official said that linking Iran’s railway network with Pakistan would benefit both countries by increasing commercial exchanges while also facilitating passenger travel between the neighboring nations.
​
Momeni announced that the modernization of the Zahedan–Mirjaveh railway line is expected to be completed within a month. He called on Pakistan to complete the standard-gauge railway from Mirjaveh to Taftan to ensure seamless train operations across the border.
​
He also said the Zahedan–Chabahar railway project is close to completion, adding that an integrated Iran-Pakistan rail network would strengthen transport links connecting South Asia with Central Asia and Europe.
​
Pakistan’s railways minister welcomed the initiative, saying Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attaches special importance to rail cooperation with Iran. Abbasi added that Pakistan’s Ministry of Railways has established a framework to advance railway projects, including the modernization of the Taftan rail line.

🇺🇦⚔️🇺🇦 What Ukrainians are saying: Syrsky's dismissal and Drapatiy's appointment

Strana's sources in military and political circles on what comes next:

➡️Zelensky didn't want to fire Syrsky. He caved not to street protests (small, no real threat) but to quiet pressure from Europe — Ukraine's main financier — pushing him to "listen to progressive forces."

➡️Zelensky has no intention of giving Drapatiy real control over the army. He's kept the Defense Ministry as his lever, refusing to bring Fedorov back there, and can go over Drapatiy's head straight to the General Staff — effectively an "Italian strike" against him if needed. Drapatiy, known for public outbursts when crossed, will likely respond in kind.

➡️Media has built Drapatiy up as "the AFU's most effective commander." Top brass disagree. Many are tied to Syrsky and hostile to Drapatiy. There are also rumors he runs a paid network of media bloggers to keep his image polished, and he's known for PR stunts.

➡️The assault regiments — the so-called "Syrsky regiments" — are a separate problem. Units like Skala are already under scrutiny for abuse of personnel, protected until now by Syrsky's cover. That cover is gone, and criminal cases are open. Expect more leaks, possibly open mutiny to media and law enforcement — from the same units currently carrying AFU offensive operations.

➡️On those so-called offensives: opinion is split between senseless losses for meaningless gains versus total exhaustion of AFU reserves. If Drapatiy scales them back, Zelensky and Syrsky will accuse him of "squandering gains."

➡️Zaluzhny's warnings about the difficulties awaiting Drapatiy make more sense now. Expect renewed pressure to reinstall Fedorov as defense minister — he's already turned down Zelensky's consolation "chief tech officer" role.

➡️Fedorov's backers are tied to US Democratic Party grant networks, now patronized by European structures, and aligned with Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau and prosecutor's office — the same networks behind last year's "cardboard Maidan." Since July 2025, when Zelensky restored the anti-corruption bodies' powers, they've hit his inner circle hard — forcing out Yermak (now under criminal investigation) and installing Fedorov and Budanov in key posts. Zelensky's camp still blocked the Kachka-Kos bill package that would've stripped him of control over security services.

➡️Last week Zelensky tried to counterpunch by firing Fedorov — then folded under pressure again. Grant-network circles now see an opening to press every remaining demand, with Fedorov as defense minister under Drapatiy as the key lever: no army control, no leverage on anything else. Zelensky's camp, plus Arakhamia's parliamentary majority, Budanov, and Poroshenko (backing Zaluzhny as a future rival to Fedorov) will resist. Not over yet.

🎙 Pentagon chief faces fierce Senate grilling over Iran war

📌 New York, IRNA – US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has faced a heated confrontation with senators during a Senate hearing over the Trump administration’s war against Iran, as lawmakers questioned the rationale for continuing the conflict and challenged Washington’s strategy toward Tehran while seeking billions of dollars in additional funding.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York pressed Hegseth over the administration’s justification for the war and challenged his previous statements about Iran’s nuclear program.
​
“The words you have used in the past don’t add up…you said that we have obliterated ‘Iran’s ability to create nuclear weapons.’ The president made the same claim. Yet, eight months later in February 2026, the president launched an active war, claiming Iran was within two weeks of having a weapon,” Gillibrand said.
​
Hegseth responded that the Iranian nuclear facilities targeted in Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 had been “completely destroyed,” but claimed that Iran had “foolishly” continued efforts to develop nuclear capabilities.
​
Gillibrand also accused Hegseth of misleading the public about the destruction of Iran’s missile-launch capabilities. Hegseth, in response, accused the senator of trying to use the issue for “campaign propaganda.”
​
In another heated exchange, Democratic Senator Gary Peters of Michigan sharply criticized the Trump administration for having no “clear winning strategy” that could plunge the United States into another “forever war”, putting American troops at risk and costing taxpayers billions of dollars.
​
Peters then questioned what the administration had achieved since the conflict began and challenged Hegseth’s request for additional funding for the Pentagon, saying it had been made despite your “failure to win this war.”
​
Hegseth responded angrily, accusing Peters of insulting US service members.
​
“I think your characterization of this incredible effort as a failure is reckless, and I think it’s irresponsible,” Hegseth said, arguing that such comments undermined the sacrifices of troops working to ensure that Iran never obtains what he described as a nuclear weapon.
​
Peters responded, saying, “Because I use the word ‘failure’ to their leaders. You sir, are the failure, not the men and women who are on that front line, not the men and women who hold up their honor with distinction, but if there’s a lack of a winning strategy, they’re in harm’s way,” according to the Hill. “You don’t have a long-term plan to actually win this war,” he added.
​
Senator Patty Murray of Washington, who is the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, also described the cost of the war with Iran as “catastrophic.” She challenged the administration’s claims that Iran’s missile capabilities have been destroyed, saying Iran is currently firing missiles at US assets.
​
Hegseth maintained that Iran was at its weakest militarily but acknowledged that it still retained capabilities. He said President Donald Trump had promised that the US would no longer fight “stupid wars” and claimed the administration was following a “realistic, America First” policy aimed at preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb.
​
The Secretary of War was quizzed by senators as the White House has requested nearly $70 billion in additional funding for the war with Iran. During the hearing, Hegseth revealed that the war has cost $37.5 billion so far.
